goal: Implement an in-repo CUDA kernel aligned with flashinfer.trtllm_fp4_block_scale_moe for real TP=1 G11 packed NVFP4 MoE, and beat FlashInfer performance.

source_state.status: Stable source is committed and pushed. No tracked kernel source diff existed before this checkpoint file.
source_state.untracked_outputs: Many generated profile/log files and an unrelated kernel_opt_fused_moe_pes directory remain untracked; they are not required for restoring the current stable code state.

recent_findings.summary: Skipping the linear mid_scale allocation, clear, or writes can look correct in a single run but later causes large GEMM2/out corruption. Keep the linear mid_scale clear/write path until the generated GEMM2 sensitivity is localized.
The current oct scatter is the best stable variant at about 224 us. x16, quad, pairload, and tile128 variants were slower or unstable.

Historical warp-shuffle GEMM2 variants were faster standalone but unstable end to end. The next useful step is a diagnostic-only tile-grid warp-shuffle wrapper plus chunked output comparison against the stable postsync GEMM2.

recommended_next_steps: Add a non-default diagnostic GEMM2 tile-grid wrapper that exposes the full v142 template parameters needed for warp-shuffle/post-load-sync experiments.
Build a chunked GEMM2 diff probe comparing stable postsync output against the warp-shuffle candidate by row_flat, local_expert, row_in_expert, column, and prepared column group.
Only promote a faster GEMM2 path after repeated end-to-end PASS results against real FlashInfer on the real G11 packed NVFP4 contract.
Large remaining gains likely require reducing GEMM2/final-scatter memory traffic, not more metadata or final-scatter micro-tuning.
